Ami Fields-Meyer is co-author with journalist Julia Angwin of “On Courage: How to Be a Dissident in an Age of Fear.” Provided photo As President Donald Trump intensifies his campaign of retribution against his political opponents and unleashes masked federal agents on immigrant communities, many American citizens are asking: What can I do? For answers, we can look to dissidents who have stood up to authoritarianism. “Authoritarianism is about stealing your rights and stealing your money,” said Ami Fields-Meyer, co-author with journalist Julia Angwin of “On Courage: How to Be a Dissident in an Age of Fear.” The authors spoke with over 100 dissidents in their research. These include a 73-year-old abortion escort in Virginia, young activists in Egypt who have challenged a dictator, students in Hong Kong defending democracy, and a civil rights lawyer who lost his job in the Trump administration while fighting for fair housing. Together, they offer a modern roadmap for resisting authoritarianism. Authoritarians start by targeting vulnerable groups, then extending to political opponents and the broader population. They say, “It’s not me who’s taking your money or your rights. This is happening because of somebody else. It’s happening because of the trans people. It’s happening because of the undocumented people,” Fields-Meyer told me. “The response has to be to expand the circle of who we are committed to.” Fields-Meyer has been a senior policy adviser to then-Vice President Kamala Harris, a senior fellow at the Harvard Kennedy School’s Allen Lab for Democracy Renovation and a strategist to national civil rights organizations and political candidates. His articles on democracy and public policy have appeared in The New Yorker, The Atlantic, The New York Times and other outlets. Ami Fields-Meyer is co-author with journalist Julia Angwin of “On Courage: How to Be a Dissident in an Age of Fear.” The authors share lessons from global dissidents. Fields-Meyer described how dissidents “repurposed their communities into extraordinarily powerful political forces. The dissident movement that helped bring down communism in Czechoslovakia was a group of theater actors (who) repurposed their theaters into organizing hubs. They stopped printing playbills on their printers and started printing protest leaflets. This is something that we see all over the world.” This includes Fields-Meyer’s home community of Brooklyn, where mutual aid groups formed during the Covid-19 pandemic are now using the same texting groups “to protect people from the federal agents who are waiting outside their doors.” Fields-Meyer said that strengthening community helps counter the ways that autocrats seek to divide people. “Authoritarianism is all about saying, ‘Don’t believe your lying eyes. You thought that you saw Renee Good shot in the street? No, you didn’t. You thought that you saw Alex Pretti shot in the street? No, you didn’t,’” said Fields-Meyer. “What we learned from Soviet dissidents is that when lies abound, you can work with other people and be with other people and be emboldened to say, ‘I do see what I see.’” “We need to be able to hold hope and hopelessness at the same time,” said Fields-Meyer. “If we do, history tells us that we’re going to win.” Latest stories Vital Communities enters talks to save town listservs from shutdown by Valley News August 26, 2026, 5:53 am UVM president says school’s budget deficit is closed despite declining enrollment by Charlotte Oliver August 25, 2026, 5:43 pm August 25, 2026, 5:47 pm As Trump tries to curtail mail-in voting, Vermont officials clean up errors on state voter rolls by Shaun Robinson August 25, 2026, 5:16 pm August 25, 2026, 5:16 pm More coverage Share your Opinion Request a correction Submit a tip Link Copy link
